title: Skull
summary: The skull is the bony case of 22 fused and joined bones that houses the brain and shapes the face.

layers.basics: The skull protects your brain and holds your eyes, ears, nose and teeth. Most of its bones are locked together by zig-zag seams.
layers.deeper: Eight cranial bones form the braincase and fourteen facial bones form the face; sutures are fibrous joints that allow growth in childhood. Holes (foramina) pass nerves and vessels, such as the foramen magnum for the spinal cord.
layers.expert: Cranial vault bones are intramembranous (dermal) while the base is largely endochondral. Sutures close variably in adulthood. Paranasal sinuses lighten the skull and the sphenoid, temporal and ethmoid bones form a complex skull base.

did_you_know: A newborn's skull has soft gaps (fontanelles) so the head can squeeze through the birth canal.

title: Mandible (jaw bone)
summary: The mandible is the only movable bone of the skull and holds the lower teeth.

layers.basics: Your lower jaw swings open and shut on hinge-like joints in front of the ears, letting you bite, chew and speak.
layers.deeper: It articulates with the temporal bone at the temporomandibular joint. Chewing muscles (masseter, temporalis) attach to it.
layers.expert: The condylar process forms a synovial joint with a fibrocartilaginous disc that permits hinge and glide movement. The inferior alveolar nerve runs within the mandibular canal.

did_you_know: The mandible is the strongest and densest bone of the face.

title: Cervical spine
summary: Seven neck vertebrae that carry the head and allow it to nod and turn.

layers.basics: The neck's seven small bones, C1 to C7, hold the head up. The top two, atlas and axis, are specially shaped so you can nod yes and shake no.
layers.deeper: Each vertebra has a body, arch and processes and the stack encloses the spinal cord. Intervertebral discs cushion the joints, and transverse foramina carry the vertebral arteries.
layers.expert: Atlanto-occipital joint supports flexion-extension, atlanto-axial joint (dens of C2) supports ~50% of cervical rotation. Cervical lordosis is a secondary curve developing as infants lift their heads.

did_you_know: Giraffes and humans both have exactly seven neck vertebrae.

title: Thoracic spine
summary: Twelve mid-back vertebrae that anchor the ribs.

layers.basics: These 12 vertebrae each hold a pair of ribs, making the upper back more rigid but giving the chest its protective cage.
layers.deeper: Facets on the vertebral bodies and transverse processes form joints with ribs. The thoracic spine has a gentle outward curve (kyphosis).
layers.expert: Rib articulations (costovertebral and costotransverse) limit motion; spinous processes slope downward and overlap. Disc height is smaller than in lumbar vertebrae.

did_you_know: Thoracic vertebrae change shape gradually, with the lower ones looking more like lumbar vertebrae.

title: Lumbar spine
summary: Five large lower-back vertebrae that bear most of the upper body's weight.

layers.basics: Your lower back has five thick vertebrae built to carry weight and bend. This area takes the strain when you lift.
layers.deeper: Large vertebral bodies and thick discs support compressive load; the inward curve (lordosis) helps balance the trunk over the pelvis.
layers.expert: Lumbar discs transmit load via nucleus pulposus hydrostatics and annulus fibrosus collagen lamellae. Spinal cord ends near L1-L2 (conus medullaris); below is the cauda equina.

did_you_know: The spinal cord ends higher than the spine does, so lumbar punctures are made below it where only nerve roots float.

title: Sacrum
summary: A wedge of five fused vertebrae that links the spine to the pelvis.

layers.basics: The sacrum is a triangle-shaped bone at the base of the spine that locks into the pelvis like a keystone.
layers.deeper: It forms joints with the two hip bones (sacroiliac joints) and has holes through which sacral nerves pass.
layers.expert: Sacral fusion completes through the late teens to the twenties; the sacral promontory is an obstetric landmark. S2-S4 supply parasympathetic outflow to pelvic organs.

did_you_know: The name 'sacrum' comes from Latin for 'sacred bone'.

title: Rib cage
summary: Twelve pairs of ribs enclose the heart and lungs and move during breathing.

layers.basics: Your ribs form a flexible cage around the heart and lungs. They swing up and out when you breathe in.
layers.deeper: The first seven pairs attach to the sternum directly via costal cartilage, pairs 8 to 10 attach indirectly, and the last two are floating.
layers.expert: 'Pump-handle' and 'bucket-handle' rib motions increase the anteroposterior and transverse diameters. Intercostal muscles stabilize and move the ribs.

did_you_know: About 1 in 200 people has an extra (cervical) rib.

title: Sternum
summary: The breastbone, a flat bone at the center of the chest.

layers.basics: The sternum is the flat bone in the middle of your chest that most of your ribs attach to.
layers.deeper: It has three parts: the manubrium, body, and the xiphoid process. It protects the heart and holds bone marrow suitable for sampling.
layers.expert: The manubriosternal joint (sternal angle) is a landmark at the level of the 2nd rib and T4/T5, where the trachea bifurcates and the aortic arch begins/ends.

did_you_know: The sternal angle is used by doctors to count ribs.

title: Pelvis
summary: A bowl of bone formed by two hip bones, the sacrum and the coccyx.

layers.basics: The pelvis carries your upper-body weight to your legs and cradles the organs of the lower abdomen.
layers.deeper: Each hip bone is made of three fused bones (ilium, ischium, pubis). The hip sockets (acetabula) hold the heads of the femurs.
layers.expert: Sex differences in pelvic inlet shape reflect obstetric adaptation; the pelvis is a compromise between bipedal locomotion and childbirth ('obstetric dilemma', debated).

did_you_know: The pelvis' shape is among the best clues to a skeleton's sex.

title: Left clavicle (collarbone)
summary: The left collarbone braces the shoulder away from the chest.

layers.basics: A slender S-shaped bone that holds your shoulder out to the side and is the one most often broken in a fall.
layers.deeper: It connects the sternum to the scapula and transmits forces from the arm to the trunk.
layers.expert: Intramembranous ossification begins here earliest, and it is the last to fuse its medial growth plate (around age 25).

did_you_know: It is one of the first bones to start ossifying in the embryo and one of the last to finish.

title: Left scapula (shoulder blade)
summary: The left shoulder blade is a flat triangle sliding over the back of the ribs.

layers.basics: A flat bone on the upper back that forms the socket of the shoulder and anchors many muscles.
layers.deeper: The glenoid cavity forms the shoulder socket; spine and acromion provide leverage for deltoid and trapezius.
layers.expert: Scapulothoracic motion contributes about one third of arm elevation (scapulohumeral rhythm ~2:1).

did_you_know: The scapula is connected to the trunk by muscles only, with no true joint to the ribs.

title: Left humerus (upper arm bone)
summary: The left humerus is the long bone of the upper arm.

layers.basics: The bone between your shoulder and elbow; its rounded top fits into the shoulder socket.
layers.deeper: The humeral head articulates with the scapula, and the distal end forms the elbow with the radius and ulna.
layers.expert: The radial nerve winds in the spiral groove of the shaft, so mid-shaft fractures may injure it.

did_you_know: The 'funny bone' is the ulnar nerve running behind the humerus, not a bone.

title: Left radius and ulna (forearm)
summary: The left forearm's two long bones allow the hand to rotate.

layers.basics: Two parallel bones between elbow and wrist. The radius crosses over the ulna when you turn your palm down.
layers.deeper: The ulna forms the main elbow hinge; the radius forms the main wrist joint. An interosseous membrane links them.
layers.expert: Pronation-supination occurs at proximal and distal radioulnar joints with the radius rotating around a fixed ulna.

did_you_know: Your forearm can turn about 180 degrees.

title: Left hand bones
summary: The left hand has 27 bones in wrist, palm and fingers.

layers.basics: Eight small wrist bones, five palm bones and fourteen finger bones give your hand fine control.
layers.deeper: Opposable thumb saddle joint allows pinch and grip.
layers.expert: Carpal arrangement in two rows; scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal and has retrograde blood supply, risking avascular necrosis.

did_you_know: Each hand holds roughly a quarter of all the body's bones.

title: Left femur (thigh bone)
summary: The left femur is the longest, strongest bone in the body.

layers.basics: The femur is your thigh bone. It must carry several times your body weight when you run or jump.
layers.deeper: Its ball-shaped head fits the hip socket; the lower end forms the knee. The neck angle is about 125 degrees.
layers.expert: Trabecular architecture aligns with principal stress trajectories; femoral neck fractures are a major osteoporosis outcome.

did_you_know: The femur's length is about a quarter of a person's height.

title: Left patella (kneecap)
summary: The left kneecap is a sesamoid bone in the quadriceps tendon.

layers.basics: A small bone in front of the knee that works as a pulley to boost the thigh muscle's pull.
layers.deeper: It increases the lever arm of the quadriceps and protects the joint.
layers.expert: The largest sesamoid bone; cartilage on its back is the thickest in the body (~5 mm).

did_you_know: Babies are born with only a cartilage kneecap that ossifies around age 3-5.

title: Left tibia and fibula (shin)
summary: The left lower-leg bones: weight-bearing tibia and slender fibula.

layers.basics: The big shin bone carries your weight and the thin outer bone mostly anchors muscles.
layers.deeper: The tibia supports about 85-90% of load while the fibula forms the outer ankle.
layers.expert: Interosseous membrane transfers load; the tibial plateau articulates with femoral condyles via menisci.

did_you_know: The fibula can be removed for bone grafts with little effect on walking.

title: Left foot bones
summary: The left foot has 26 bones forming arches.

layers.basics: Your foot's arches work like springs: they absorb landing and push you forward.
layers.deeper: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges form medial longitudinal, lateral and transverse arches.
layers.expert: The plantar fascia and 'windlass mechanism' stiffen the foot during push-off; the calcaneus is the largest tarsal.

did_you_know: Humans have arched feet unlike any other ape.

title: Long bone (structure)
summary: A long bone has a hard outer shell, a spongy interior and a marrow cavity.

layers.basics: A long bone is hard on the outside, like a tube, and honeycombed at the ends, which keeps it strong yet light.
layers.deeper: The shaft (diaphysis) is mostly compact bone around a marrow cavity; the ends (epiphyses) hold spongy bone and are capped with cartilage.
layers.expert: Compact bone is organized into osteons (Haversian systems); spongy bone is a lattice of trabeculae oriented along stress lines; the periosteum supplies osteoprogenitors; growth plates add length until closure.

did_you_know: Bone is about as strong as cast iron for its weight in compression but much lighter.

title: Compact bone
summary: Dense bone forming the outer shell.

layers.basics: The hard, smooth outer layer that gives bone its strength.
layers.deeper: Built from cylinders called osteons with a central canal carrying vessels.
layers.expert: Lamellae of mineralized collagen surround Haversian canals, linked by Volkmann's canals; osteocytes in lacunae communicate via canaliculi.

facts: Dense bone forming the outer shell
did_you_know: Osteons are tiny: dozens fit in a pinhead cross-section.

title: Spongy (cancellous) bone
summary: A lattice of thin struts at the bone ends.

layers.basics: A honeycomb inside the ends of bones that makes them light and shock-absorbing.
layers.deeper: Trabeculae align along stress; marrow fills the gaps.
layers.expert: Higher surface-to-volume ratio gives it ~8× the remodeling turnover of cortical bone.

facts: A lattice of thin struts at the bone ends
did_you_know: Spongy bone is renewed far faster than compact bone.

title: Bone marrow
summary: Soft tissue inside bones that makes blood cells.

layers.basics: Red marrow produces blood cells; yellow marrow stores fat.
layers.deeper: Hematopoietic stem cells in marrow niches give rise to red cells, white cells and platelets.
layers.expert: Adults produce ≈ 2×10^11 red cells and ≈ 10^11 platelets and neutrophils daily; niches involve CXCL12-abundant reticular cells and osteoblasts.

facts: Soft tissue inside bones that makes blood cells
did_you_know: Your marrow makes about 2 million red blood cells every second.

title: Periosteum
summary: A tough membrane covering the outer bone.

layers.basics: The skin of the bone: tough, full of nerves and blood vessels, and key to bone healing.
layers.deeper: It supplies cells and blood to the bone and anchors tendons.
layers.expert: Inner cambium layer contains osteoprogenitors; Sharpey's fibres anchor tendons to bone; richly innervated, hence the pain of fractures.

facts: A tough membrane covering the outer bone
did_you_know: Bone breaks hurt largely because the periosteum is packed with nerves.

title: Growth plate (epiphyseal plate)
summary: A cartilage disc that lets a growing bone lengthen.

layers.basics: Children grow taller because cartilage here keeps being made and then turned into bone.
layers.deeper: Cells stack in columns, enlarge, die and are replaced by bone. It closes after puberty.
layers.expert: Zones: resting, proliferative, hypertrophic and calcification; regulated by GH/IGF-1, sex steroids, thyroid hormone, and Ihh/PTHrP.

facts: A cartilage disc that lets a growing bone lengthen
did_you_know: Growth plates are the weakest part of a child's skeleton.

title: Synovial joint
summary: A joint with a fluid-filled capsule that lets bones slide smoothly.

layers.basics: A freely movable joint, like your knee or shoulder, where slippery cartilage and fluid cut friction to almost nothing.
layers.deeper: Cartilage caps the bones, a capsule makes lubricating synovial fluid, and ligaments stabilize the joint. Types include hinge, ball-and-socket, pivot and saddle.
layers.expert: Friction coefficients of about 0.001-0.01 arise from boundary lubrication (lubricin, hyaluronan) and fluid-film mechanisms. Cartilage lacks blood vessels and is nourished by loading-driven diffusion.

did_you_know: Joint cartilage can be slipperier than ice on ice.
